Taiwan Roam ｜ Outlying Islands War-Heritage Special Issue

Through the "Kinmen-Matsu Award" Army Ghost Lore and Peaceful Sea Breezes: An In-Depth Guide to the Battlefield Secrets of Kinmen & Matsu, Granite Tunnels, and Blue Tears

From Cold War Ghost Lore to Transquil Island Breezes: Subterranean Canals, Costa Citades & The Living History
Zenium The Island's Past and Present: The Frontline Fortress of the Cold War

Kinmen and Matsu, two granite archipelagos scattered on the western side of the Taiwan Strait and hugging the Min River estuary and Xiamen Bay, were once the fiercest frontline outposts of the Cold War. From the 1949 Battle of Guningtou to the 1958 Second Taiwan Strait Crisis, the baptism of hundreds of thousands of shells forged this land into an "underground steel fortress."

Yet as the smoke of war faded and military control was lifted, what now unfolds before travelers is the world's densest network of granite underground wonders, the static anti-landing rail stakes against the sunset, the stone houses of Qinbi Village nestled between mountain and sea, and the breathtaking "Blue Tears" lapping the shore on early summer nights.

Zenium Elders' Teatime Topics: From the "Kinmen-Matsu Award" Army Ghost Lore to the Gentle Sea Breeze of Peace

Ever since childhood, whenever elders gathered over tea during holidays, the conversation would invariably wander back to those absurd and bittersweet memories of serving in the military on Kinmen and Matsu.

In the era of compulsory military service, being "drawn to an outlying island" was jokingly called winning the "Kinmen-Matsu Award"—a byword for parents wiping away tears at the Keelung dock and conscripts feeling a chill in their hearts. What followed were countless army ghost stories spread across Taiwan: eerie cries from the sea during midnight sentry duty, unknown footsteps deep within abandoned tunnels when fog blanketed the islands, mysterious sealed Zhongshan rooms, and decrepit barracks draped in camouflage netting. In the vivid storytelling of the older generation, Kinmen and Matsu were shrouded in a veil of mystery and dread in many people's childhood memories.

But once you truly set foot on this land, you will find that the fears of the past have transformed into the most moving scenery and charm.

The legendary "ghost cries" were actually the howling of fierce northeast monsoon winds rushing through granite sea caves on winter nights; the dark tunnels that chilled recruits to the bone were survival miracles carved inch by inch from solid granite by the blood, sweat, and pickaxes of countless young men. Today, the anti-landing rail stakes stand silently on the golden sands revealed at low tide, forming the most beautiful and desolate silhouettes against the sunset; wild lilies and blanket flowers bloom across abandoned artillery positions, and the once-intimidating broadcasting wall now plays Teresa Teng's tender songs.

Even though some corners of the islands still hold mottled abandoned bunkers and desolate old houses, there is no need to feel afraid when visiting Kinmen and Matsu. These legends and ghost stories are not meant to frighten travelers, but are the scars and medals left behind by time. Every dim tunnel and every ivy-covered air-raid shelter silently tells of the youth of the soldiers who once defended these islands, and stands as the most precious historical witness to how the two sides moved from the smoke of war toward peace and tranquility.

Taiwan Roam ｜ The Ultimate 100-Peak Expedition

Above the Sea of Clouds Beyond Mount Fuji: The Ultimate Hiking Guide to Taiwan's Yushan, the 100 High Peaks, and the "Angel's Tear" Jiaming Lake

Nordheast Asia's Crown Summit (3,952m), The Angel's Tear (3,310m) & The 3,000-Meter Alpine Realm
Zenium The Island's Geological Myth: 268 Three-Thousand-Meter Peaks Towering Above Mount Fuji

Many international hikers can hardly imagine that Taiwan, a mere 36,000 square kilometers, is home to 268 lofty peaks exceeding 3,000 meters (about 9,843 feet). Compared with Japan, which has only Mount Fuji and a handful of peaks above 3,000 meters, Taiwan's highest summit—Yushan Main Peak (3,952 m / 12,966 ft), towers nearly 200 meters above Japan's highest peak, Mount Fuji (3,776 m), making it the veritable "highest peak in Northeast Asia."

The intense collision of the Eurasian and Philippine Sea plates has sculpted this island's astonishing vertical terrain: departing from a tropical coast, a drive of just a few hours brings you to subalpine conifer forests and alpine tundra, spanning an ecological gradient equivalent to that from the equator to the Arctic Circle.

Zenium A Traveler's Heartfelt Prose: The Sapphire Miracle at 3,000 Meters—A Journey to Jiaming Lake and the Xiangyang Peaks

In Taiwan's hiking community, there is a mysterious mirror hidden on a 3,000-meter ridge in the southern Central Mountain Range—the ultimate pilgrimage site in the hearts of countless mountaineers:Taitung's Jiaming Lake (3,310 m). As Taiwan's second-highest alpine lake, it is hailed as the "Angel's Tear 💧," and when you stand by its shore, it resembles a pristine oval sapphire set in an endless emerald expanse of arrow bamboo meadow!

We set out in the crisp, clear autumn, starting from the Xiangyang trailhead. To let our bodies gradually acclimate to the high-altitude pressure and avoid acute mountain sickness, we usually arranged a three-day, two-night trip (or a more leisurely four-day, three-night one) staying at the Xiangyang and Jiaming Lake mountain huts. Climbing at a steady pace not only lets you greet the golden sunrise rolling up from the Pacific at dawn, but also lets you quietly admire the ever-changing, breathtaking sea of clouds—without climbing too fast.

Along the Jiaming Lake traverse, there is also the chance to climb two of Taiwan's most representative 100 peaks: the majestic and soaring Xiangyang Mountain (3,603 m) and the vast, rolling Sancha Mountain (3,496 m). Coming here in person was a precious and beautiful memory. We came in autumn, and the weather was fine all the way, but on the morning we reached Jiaming Lake a thick fog suddenly rolled in, and we all thought we wouldn't see the lake, our disappointment hard to hide. Yet the moment we climbed up, the sky suddenly cleared, and a fierce wind swept the clouds away, allowing us to admire the entire deep-blue, pristine oval sapphire in full! The miraculous clearing lasted only half an hour before swiftly turning back into a white wall. We are deeply grateful to the heavens for this unforgettable, beautiful gift.

⚠️ High-Altitude Acclimatization and Safety Rules: Above 3,000 meters, atmospheric pressure and oxygen content are only about 65% of sea level.Never attempt a single-day summit push of Yushan or Jiaming Lake directly from sea level. Be sure to spend the previous night acclimatizing at Alishan (2,200 m), Tataka (2,600 m), or Xiangyang (2,300 m). Mountain weather changes many times a day, and afternoon fog and thunderstorms can easily cause hypothermia; while hiking, follow the golden rule of "summit by noon, retreat to the hut by afternoon."

(as low as -2°C at night)		 Alpine azaleas bloom in the chilly spring air. From mid-May the plum-rain season brings continuous rain that makes trails muddy, with occasional leftover snow and black ice. From March to early April, shady high-altitude slopes still hold hard snow and ice, so light crampons are recommended as backup; after May, crampons are unnecessary.
Summer (Afternoon Thunderstorms) June – August 6°C ~ 16°C
(4°C – 8°C at night)		 Sunlight is intense. Violent heat-convection thunderstorms often erupt after 1:00 p.m. daily. July–August is the peak typhoon season in the western Pacific (mountains close immediately when a typhoon warning is issued). No crampons needed. The core is 100% waterproof rain jacket and pants plus a backpack rain cover; never wear ordinary thin ponchos, which cause dampness and hypothermia.
Autumn (★ the Best Golden Season) September – November 2°C - 10°C
(-4°C to 2°C at night)		 The atmosphere is stable and rainy days are the fewest of the year! Visibility is superb, making it easiest to admire Jiaming Lake's sapphire-like mirror reflections and the rolling sea of clouds. No crampons needed. Dress warmly and block the wind (800-fill down jacket + windproof warm hat); the wind-chill is severe at dawn.
Winter (Snow & Ice Season) December – February - 10°C. - 4°C.
(as low as -12°C at night)		 Under the influence of continental cold air masses, the Yushan wind gap to the summit, the Xueshan cirque, and Hehuan Wuling often snow and ice over, with iron chains on the cliffs completely frozen (black ice). Carrying 10/12-point professional mountaineering crampons is mandatory. National parks impose "snow-season control" and check crampons, ice axes, and helmets at the trailhead; simple six-point or chain crampons are prohibited!

Zenium A Traveler's Journal: From Shoreline Snorkeling to Deep-Diving Vistas—Discovering the Surprises and Warmth of Northern Taiwan's Underwater World

When I first learned to snorkel, I always thought diving required flying far away to the outlying islands or Kenting, never realizing northern Taiwan has such wonderful dive sites! Later I discovered that every summer, so many friends around me were learning freediving on the Northeast Coast. While simply floating on the surface may not reveal schools of fish as spectacular as imagined, the moment you switch to scuba gear or dive deep in one breath, the underwater view is entirely different—the thrill of being surrounded by three-dimensional sea-cliff walls, gorgonian corals, and vast schools of fish is truly unlike anything else.

And beyond diving, the north coast's intertidal ecology is astonishingly rich! I once saw round little pufferfish and slowly crawling sea cucumbers up close in the shallow reef pools along the shore—fascinating to observe. This area is also wonderful for bringing kids to play in the water and learn about the ocean: "Longdong Four Seasons Bay" has excellent facilities and professional lifeguards on duty, and Keelung's "Heping Island Geopark" is a favorite among parents, with dedicated shallow paddling pools and safe sand-play areas for children, and even the deep snorkeling zone is securely roped off for complete peace of mind. The only thing to note is that on days with bigger swells, floating on the surface for too long can leave you slightly tipsy with "sea sickness," so bring motion-sickness pills to enjoy it to the fullest!

The Shape of Wind and the Giant-Tree Forest: A Three-Day, Two-Night Private Hsinchu Map—Visiting the Prayer-Fulfilling City God Temple, Coastal Wind-Turbine Bike Paths, Jianshi Hot Springs & Camping, and the Smangus Divine Trees

Zenium A Traveler's Journal: The Windy City's Deep Affection—Devout Prayers at the City God Temple, the Coastal Green Tunnel, and a Dozen Wild Camping Trips to Jianshi

Every year, our family makes a special trip to pray at the Hsinchu City God Temple and the Chihfu Wangye Shrine. This bond runs especially deep—back when I was praying for a child, and even for fulfilling my vows after safely giving birth, I came here to earnestly pray to Chihfu Wangye. Though Taiwan has many famous temples for seeking children, in my heart I have always favored this Hsinchu shrine with its flourishing incense and profound blessings.

Many people's first impression of Hsinchu is Taiwan's semiconductor hub—the high-tech city with the highest prices and housing costs in Taiwan. But once you step deeper into this "Windy City," you'll find it hides an astonishing wealth of authentic cuisine and deep cultural heritage. Our family loves cycling in Hsinchu along the 17-kilometer coastal bike path, flanked by secret green tunnels, where the sea breeze carries you past giant wind turbines slowly turning where sea meets sky—the views are simply vast.

Family life in Hsinchu is also wonderfully rich! Downtown has the compact, refined, and clean Hsinchu Zoo—a favorite place we often take the kids; there's also the vast outdoor lawn of Qingqing Grassland, where children can run freely and fly kites in the wind, surrounded by plenty of family-friendly cafés and brunch spots with delicious food.

Besides the city and the coast, our family heads to Jianshi Township almost every year, where we've soaked in natural hot springs and camped in the mountains nearly a dozen times! Along the highway we visit Neiwan Old Street, watching painted trains slowly pass along the retro branch line—the wooden mountain-town scenery is full of character. By early summer you can also see fireflies scattered across the hillsides. For hiking enthusiasts, Jianshi offers many wildly charming trails; and the "Smangus" and "Zhensibao" giant ancient red-cypress trees towering above the sea of clouds are hallowed, reservation-required mountain-entry sites. Standing beneath these millennia-old trees, you'll be utterly awed by Taiwan's magnificent natural wonders!

 1. Jiaoxi Hot Spring Waterparks

 Jiaoxi is home to Taiwan’s premier odorless, skin-smoothing sodium bicarbonate "Beauty Springs". Top family resorts like Evergreen Resort Hotel and Chuan-Tang Spring feature epic hot spring waterslides, hydrotherapy jets, and doctor fish pools.

 2. Surfing & SUP at Wushi Harbor

 Wushi Harbor and Waiao Beach in Toucheng offer gentle sand-bottom swells, perfect for beginner surfing and SUP paddleboarding. English-friendly shops like G-Cool and Sweet Potato Surf offer boards and guided coaching.

 3. Glamping Overlooking the Plain

All told, I've truly been to Yilan more than fifty times. In the early days, my main reason was to race out of the Hsuehshan Tunnel straight to Jiaoxi for a natural beauty bath and to feast on local traditional snacks; but these past few years, the way I enjoy Yilan has changed a lot. The most charming thing about Yilan is that its seaside activities keep getting better—whether SUP paddleboarding or surfing at Wushi Harbor's Wai'ao, you feel the full vitality of the Pacific.

Now I seek to be even closer to nature. Camping in Yilan is thriving, and many campsites now boast million-dollar night views overlooking the lights of the Lanyang Plain. Just sitting before your tent watching the starry sky and the plain's nightscape, with the cool mountain breeze, all the anxiety built up in the city simply melts away. Yilan's greatest charm is its truly beautiful mountains and waters—aptly Taipei's irreplaceable "backyard garden."

After having kids, Yilan became our family paradise. There are rich family farms where children can get up close with capybaras and sika deer, plus many specialty brunch spots and designer cafés tucked among the fields. During the day, enjoy a hearty, warm brunch with the whole family; in the afternoon, check in to a family resort with its own large hot-spring waterslide, watching the kids slide and play in the spring with endless laughter—this is my idea of the perfect vacation.

Weekend Hop Vol. 07 ｜ In-Depth Slow-Living Field Report

Crashing Swells and Marble Cliffs: A Three-Day, Two-Night Private Hualien Map—Qixingtan Pebbles, the Secret Face-Profile Rock, Indigenous Wood-Firing & Sea-View Coffee

Where Mountains Plumet into Waves: Marble Gorges, Face Rock Security & Indigenous Hearth
Zenium A Traveler's Journal: From Wild Cliff Adventures to Watching Waves with the Kids—The Island's Most Foreign-Like Secluded Haven

In recent years, every time I set foot in Hualien, I often get a strange feeling—this place really doesn't feel like the Taiwan I remember. The streets and trails are full of European and American backpackers, and with so many languages around me, I can't help but wonder, "Did I accidentally leave the country?"

Before we had kids, a Hualien trip meant a purely wild route—I loved driving straight to the Hualien-Taitung sea cliffs or into the deep mountains in search of emerald waterfalls and pools, seeking visual and spiritual adventure. Now with children, the pace has slowed; we prefer renting a scooter or booking a charter to ride the coastline with the kids, sip coffee and sea breeze at Hayaku, and sit on Qixingtan's pebble beach listening to the long waves wash over the stones. Hualien's family-friendly offerings these past years are truly impressive—"Yunshanshui Dream Lake" never fails to amaze me, with bald cypresses reflecting on Tiffany-blue water; strolling and cycling there with the kids, happiness wells up naturally.

For hiking enthusiasts, Hualien is heaven. Trek to the Taiwanchi camp or even venture to the mysterious Qilai Lake; the majestic, mountain-embraced grandeur makes it hard to believe this small island hides such towering scenery—exactly why I eagerly recommend it to foreign friends! In addition, Chihnan National Forest Recreation Area is lush and serene, while Fengbin's Dashibi Mountain trail is a less-crowded sea-view secret; when self-driving, definitely stop to summit and overlook the curved bay.

During the pandemic, I even spent a whole week at Fengbin's "Alpine Forest Base," far from the city's noise, quietly savoring Taiwan's pristine natural beauty—even briefly dreaming, "It would be wonderful to live here after retirement." Though eastern Taiwan has many earthquakes, it is undeniably the purest and most beautiful part of Taiwan. The Amis people's traditional sea ritual grounds are also a highly representative cultural landscape, and I strongly recommend joining if you get the chance. Hidden here is the adventure path to the secret "Face-Profile Rock"—descend behind the sea-ritual pavilion and cross the silver-grass thicket for about 10 minutes to arrive, but watch out for the sharp reef rocks; another route goes from Dasheng Temple down to the coast, heading north on the left, about 25 minutes longer, but the intertidal wonders along the way are well worth exploring.

Tainan is a city I must visit every year, and each visit must last a full three days and two nights to be satisfying. As Taiwan's historic capital, Tainan's homestays are full of soul. Many old houses, after renovation, retain their old-time wooden windows and terrazzo floors while incorporating modern comfort—the retro, serene feeling at check-in is especially charming. Tainan also has many richly cultured tea houses and independent cafés, and every visit I pack my schedule with tea and café hopping; even souvenir shopping is excellent, leaving each time with arms full. I'm also especially fond of Tainan's traditional noodle shops, whose astonishing variety of noodle dishes each boast a unique minced-pork and broth recipe.

Since having kids, our itinerary has extended to the suburbs. Tainan's coast and evening sunsets are truly perfect for children—gentle waters and wide beaches; plus the Chimei Museum's Western-art castle and Hayashi Department Store's retro space. Weekend Hop Vol. 05 ｜ In-Depth Slow-Living Field Report

A Mountain-Sea Corridor Carved by the Sea Breeze: A One-Day Charter of the North Coast & Jiufen—Rock Formations, Sanzhi Sea-View Coffee, Old-Street Tea & Guihou Seafood

Wind, Waves & Granite: An Unhurried Costa Drive Acros Yehliu, Jiufen and Wild Capes
Zenium A Traveler's Journal: Slow Time Between Mountains and Sea—Tea, Sunsets, and Breezy North Coast Memories

The Jiufen of old and the Jiufen of today really differ greatly. Early on there were many original shops full of local character; now that tourists have multiplied, most goods lean toward tourism. Yet even as the commercial feel deepens, Jiufen's most irreplaceable and breathtaking feature remains that stunning scenery where mountains meet the sea.

Brewing tea at A-Mei Tea House was something I first tried while hosting Japanese friends in Taiwan. Had it not been for entertaining foreign guests, I might never have stepped inside on my own; but that time, we sat by the window and learned the traditional steps of warming the pot, adding leaves, savoring the aroma, and tasting, spending a wonderfully relaxing afternoon. The moment we walked out to greet the sunset and saw the sky dyed red over Shen'ao Bay, I marveled at how beautiful Taiwan is! That vast interweaving of mountains and sea even gives locals the illusion of being on vacation abroad. Now many quality independent cafés have opened in Jiufen's mountain town, and when you're tired from shopping, it's a pleasure to find a quiet scenic seat for coffee and sea views.

I also love Sanzhi, a coastal town I never tire of. Living in Taipei, when I don't want to go far but crave a drive and sea views, I enjoy driving to Sanzhi's coastal cafés any time of year, even winter. Whenever I want to see the sea, I find a comfortable café, order a pour-over, eat and drink, read a book, or open my laptop to work. On holidays I bring the family to the beach; Sanzhi's coast is now better planned and more family-friendly, with foot-rinse and sand-wash facilities, family-designed meals and sand-play areas—even perfect for walking the dog.

Guihou Fishing Harbor is a place I return to every summer without fail, where feasting on freshly caught and steamed Wanli crab is a must; after eating, I bring the kids to the intertidal zone, where spotting sea slaters, hermit crabs, and big crabs in the rock crevices makes them jump and cheer with excitement! The Shuinandong Yin-Yang Sea and the Thirteen Levels ruins are also highly educational secret spots—each time we drive past, the yellow-blue colors of the Yin-Yang Sea look completely different depending on weather, light, and mineral water flow, and the kids always ask why, while even foreign visitors marvel. Walking down to observe the weathered sedimentary rocks up close, their distinct layers and fine textures make me think the golden-brown slabs really look just like freshly baked croissants!

Zenium Mountain-Sea Corridor: Eons of Weathered Rock Formations, a Two-Toned Bay, and the Gold-Rush Mountain Town

Heading north out of Taipei, in under an hour's drive the city's concrete jungle instantly gives way to the majestic coastline where the Pacific meets the East China Sea. Sculpted over millions of years by the northeast monsoon and ocean waves,Yehliu Geoparkhas produced the world-renowned mushroom rocks, honeycomb rocks, and the Queen's Head wonder; continuing along Provincial Highway 2 toward Sanzhi and Jinshan lies Taipei's all-season seaside backyard.

As the road winds into the Ruifang mountains, once bustling with gold and copper mines,Jiufen and Jinguashicome into view. At the foot of the mountain,the Shuinandong Yin-Yang Sea—where iron-pyrite-rich streams from the Jinguashi hills flow into the bay, weaving golden and sapphire blue into a magical two-tone gradient. The thousand-layered weathered sandstone along the shore, whose texture resembles a "croissant," paired with the imposing "Thirteen Levels Ruins (Shuinandong Smelter)" halfway up the hill, form a natural tableau of striking visual drama and geological significance.

Weekend Hop Vol. 04 ｜ Taiwan Deep Travel · Slow-Living Field Report

A Symphony of Lane Pulses and Skylines: A Three-Day, Two-Night Private Taipei Map Through Old-House Cafés, Anime Tech, and Lunar New Year Markets

Taipei Symphony: A Curaed 72-Hour Guide to Heritage Lanes, Modern Lights & Culinary Craft
Zenium Traveler's Notes: Lunar New Year Spirit, Tech-Industry Memories, and Holiday Shop-Hopping in Taipei

Many foreign friends first meet Taipei through the New Year's Eve fireworks at Taipei 101, the giant fried chicken at Shilin Night Market, or the world-class treasures at the National Palace Museum. But if you ask me where this city's most irreplaceable soul lives, I would unhesitatingly point to those old districts and creative cultural clusters etched with traces of everyday life.

Dadaocheng and Dihua Street are places I make sure to visit every year before Lunar New Year. Honestly, the festive spirit in downtown Taipei has faded over the years, but the moment you step into Dihua Street before the holiday, that lively clamor unique to Taiwan's traditional festivals washes over you. The whole street is packed yet joyful, with shopkeepers and vendors warmly urging everyone to sample food and drink hot soup; charcoal-grilled mullet roe, armloads of holiday candies, and freshly grilled squid strips that grow sweeter the more you chew—every bite is irresistible. That human warmth, the wok-fired market bustle, and the festive temperature are truly a "glory of Taiwan" worth proudly recommending to the world.

Chifeng Street and the Zhongshan-Shuanglian creative district, on the other hand, hold a particularly dear personal memory—this is where I clocked in every day during my tech-industry years. Back then, even while passing through daily, I couldn't help but peek at which charming new shop had opened. Sometimes I would even take a weekday-afternoon leave just to dodge the holiday crowds and leisurely line up in Chifeng Street for freshly fried crispy doughnuts, find a cozy Japanese bistro, or duck into an old-house café for a pour-over. The alleys here are narrow and the shops tiny—dining can feel a bit cramped—but every corner is thoughtfully designed and utterly photogenic. Today, the area around Zhongshan MRT Station has become the favorite district of the younger generation; prices have risen, but stylish cafés keep opening one after another, always brimming with vitality.

I also love taking the MRT to Zhongxiao Xinsheng Station on my days off. In the past, I spent nearly every holiday at Huashan 1914 Creative Park—finding a quiet café to sit, browsing independent design exhibitions or market events; after a stroll, I'd wander along the path into Syntrend Creative Park to check out the latest tech products, spin a few freshly stocked Japanese gachapon, and admire the anime figures filling the display windows. With no need to rush, I can easily spend a whole day in the Zhongxiao Xinsheng area, fully immersed in my own slow-living world.

To roam Taipei over 72 hours, the most enchanting way is to experience three utterly different dimensions of life along the city's timeline:

Dadaocheng (Datong District)preserves the bustling tea and fabric trade of a century ago. Under the Baroque facades and arcades, dried goods, mullet roe, and herbal aromas waft in the breeze; stroll onward toChifeng Street (Zhongshan District), where old blacksmith shops and auto-repair hardware stores have transformed into the highest-density cluster of stylish cafés and vintage boutiques in Taiwan; take the MRT toZhongxiao Xinsheng Station, where the red-brick warehouses of Huashan 1914, converted from a Japanese-era winery, face Syntrend Creative Park across the street—anime figures, ichiban-kuji gachapon, and tech product showcases reveal Taipei's vibrant, inclusive spirit.

Weekend Hop Vol. 03 ｜ Taiwan Deep Travel · Slow-Living Field Report

Rise of the Harbor & Its Ocean Soul: From Heavy-Industry Docks to a Cultural Waterfront—Kaohsiung's Port-City Economic Pulse and Arts Slow-Travel

Tides of Transport: The Economic Response, Port Architecture & Cultural Pulse of Kaohsiung
Zenium Traveler's Notes: From Youthful Exhibition-Hopping to Family Bike Rides—Fully Unwinding in Southern Taiwan's Warmth

Back in my student days, visiting Kaohsiung was always full of youthful curiosity—an eagerness to dive into bustling shopping districts, catch large art exhibitions, or hop a ferry to Qijin to feel the sea breeze on the beach.

But as my life has changed over the years, I've grown increasingly enchanted by the Kaohsiung of today. On every visit, I love holding my family's hand while strolling the Pier-2 Art Center, or looping around a few new department stores to rent bikes and ride along the wide, gentle tree-lined and harbor trails. In summer especially, Kaohsiung often sets up many free water parks and splash facilities—safe, clean, and thoughtful—a true family paradise where kids can burn off energy and adults can truly relax.

Many people ask if I only visit night markets when in Kaohsiung. Actually, I rarely go to night markets. Because Kaohsiung's sun is fierce and temperatures run high, with elders and kids in tow we almost always pick specialty restaurants and stylish cafés instead. Kaohsiung's restaurants and cafés share one enviable trait—"spaces are spacious, airy, high-ceilinged, with wide, comfortable seating"—strollers glide in without feeling cramped, the air conditioning is cool and pleasant, and it's extremely family-friendly! Even better, the high-star hotels and boutique stays here offer exceptional value, far more affordable than the north, and with a dense MRT and light-rail network, hauling around bags is never a worry.

Every Kaohsiung itinerary we plan always reserves a full day to take the kids to SKM Park Outlets (Caogandao) for its outdoor theme park, then head to Sizihwan for the sunset in the evening; sometimes we drive or charter south toward Dapeng Bay, where the wide lagoon road and endless sea-and-sky views unfold—riding along the coast, that expansive vista opens your whole heart.

But what makes Kaohsiung hardest to leave is always its "people." The locals are warm, kind, and easygoing from the heart—whether it's the shopkeepers' friendly greetings when you ask for directions, or the smiles on hotel staff and drivers. The moment you step onto this sun-warmed land, travel fatigue and accumulated stress melt away. In Kaohsiung, your mood shifts instantly, and you can't help but fall deeply in love with the city's people, places, and things, and with the south's purest heartfelt warmth.

Zenium Urban Fabric: How Did a Heavy-Industry Steel City Become a Marine Arts Waterfront?

The former "Takao Port" built its world standing on ship-breaking, heavy industry, and handling half of Taiwan's containers. The tall coastal walls and restricted zones once cut citizens off from the sea; today those walls are fully torn down, and the old harbor railway has become Taiwan's first circular waterfront light rail, whisking travelers seamlessly toKaohsiung Music CenterI don't know.the Port Terminalandthe Grand Harbor Bridge。

The old harbor warehouses, once used to store sugar and fishmeal during the Japanese era, now host original design brands, independent bookstores, and music performance spaces. Every afternoon at 3 PM, the Grand Harbor Bridge—Asia's longest horizontal rotating bridge—slowly rotates 90 degrees over the water, completing the city's most ceremonial harbor slow-living scene.

Weekend Hop Vol. 02 ｜ Taiwan Deep Travel · Slow-Living Field Report

A Blue Retreat on Rippling Waters: Sun Moon Lake Loop Buses, the World's Most Beautiful Bike Path, and a Deep Thao-Culture Journey

Security in Azure: A Discerning Guide to Sun Moon Lake's Waterside Architecture, Cycling Soul & Thao Heritage
Zenium Traveler's Notes: Into Shuishalian's Dawn and Dusk, Camping, and a Wonderland of Mountains and Water

Sun Moon Lake is one of Taiwan's most beautiful places, and for many foreign visitors it's the first stop they insist on. If you only have a single day, it's actually very convenient to charter over from Taichung; swap into a comfortable pair of walking shoes and you can leisurely circle the lakeside trail.

The lakeside trail here is one of my favorite places to exercise and hike—lush vegetation lines both sides, with the clear, emerald deep lake beside you and the light clink of bicycle chains drifting by, your body and mind instantly relax. If you're bringing kids, it's also perfect to bring bikes along and let them ride freely on the gentle waterside path.

In my memory, "camping" is absolutely the deepest way to experience Sun Moon Lake's beauty. Autumn here is breathtaking—the mountains are layered in gold and warm brown, the lake mirrors the fall colors, and the whole valley looks like a still oil painting. Most unforgettable are the open-air cooking moments at the campsite—steam rising from the pot, people strolling the lakefront with the breeze, the afternoon sun quietly falling on the rippling water, sparkling like scattered diamonds. After the meal, holding my family's hand as we walk the trail and chat—that peaceful, unhurried beauty is truly unforgettable.

Taiwan's greatest blessing is its mild year-round climate; Sun Moon Lake never freezes even in winter, so it's always comforting to visit in any season. It's not only perfect for vacation and relaxation but also an outstanding outdoor sports venue—besides hiking and biking, the calm lake is ideal for SUP paddleboarding and canoeing, and each year it even hosts the spectacular, island-wide "Sun Moon Lake Swimming Carnival," an international event!

When dusk falls and daytime crowds disperse, Sun Moon Lake turns into a fairyland at night—utterly serene, with a brilliant, light-pollution-free starry sky overhead. Walk over to the nearby food street, whose snacks are among the few places I feel don't just sell the same generic fare found all over Taiwan. Freshly steamed and pounded handmade mochi are soft and chewy, and tea eggs simmered in local black tea carry an especially rich, deep flavor—full of local character. One reminder: because the lake is humid, temperatures can drop sharply and feel especially cold and damp at night, so be sure to bring a windproof, warm jacket for evening strolls.

Zenium Lake Water, Light, and the Shuishe Dam: CNN's Stunning Global Waterfront Bike Route

The Sun Moon Lake lakeside bike path was once named one of the "world's top ten most beautiful bike paths" by CNN. Spanning about 30 km, its crown jewel runs fromShuishe Visitor Center to Xiangshan Visitor Center—a roughly 3.4 km stretch of waterside bike path. From 6:30 to 8:00 AM is the purest moment along this shore, when the lake is as still as a mirror and thin mist wraps Lalu Island in the lake's center.

Riding pastthe Shuishe Dam boardwalk, the railing-free wooden planks bring the emerald water right before your eyes; at the finish lies the Xiangshan Administration and Visitor Center, designed by Japanese master architect Kiyoshi Sey TakeyamaXiangshan Administration & Visitor Center, whose unfinished-board-formed concrete lines embrace the lake like open hands. The two buildings stretch a 34-meter column-free span, and the central infinity pool reflects sky and lake—a perfect midway point to settle the mind.

Zenium Traveler's Notes: I've Been to Alishan Countless Times, and Every Visit Brings New Insight

I've been to Alishan many times—from going alone, to traveling with companions, to now holding my child's hand—and each trip up the mountain feels completely different. When I was younger, I always rushed to chase the dawn, believing that seeing the first rays of the new year light up the mountain was a powerful, beautiful beginning.

Now with a family, I prefer taking the kids camping in Alishan, truly immersed in the forest's phytoncides and nature. Honestly, the mountain roads up here are genuinely challenging, and the road conditions and scenery change with every visit; but it's precisely while winding through the layered forest roads—whether driving myself or booking a charter—that you feel nature's grandeur and mystery more deeply.

The mountain weather shifts rapidly. I remember one February trip—the night was freezing, but stepping out for a walk, the sky was crystal clear and the stars so pure they looked like scattered diamonds. I eagerly awaited a brilliant sunrise, only to be met with fine drizzle at dawn. That day we walked the Alishan trails in raincoats; though the ground was wet and cold, the rain-soaked Alishan was breathtakingly beautiful—like stepping into a Studio Ghibli dream forest, with crisp birdsong and air full of fresh moisture. On the trails, where vehicles are completely banned, there was only a rare stillness, and all the accumulated irritations and distractions in my mind were washed away in an instant. That's why, every year, I long to return here to "purify" myself once again.

Besides alpine camping and tea-garden strolls, we always sample the mountain wild vegetables and indigenous wood-fired cuisine; taking the kids to Fenqihu is also a reserved ritual—there's the old train they adore and plenty of free, leisurely spots. Hand in hand along the tracks beside the railway crossing, watching the little train pass by, the air carries the distinctive cypress aroma of the old buildings; in the afternoon, we gaze out at the rolling Alishan sea of clouds—truly Taiwan's most spectacular sight, as if the whole body were gently resting atop a bed of clouds. I strongly recommend staying a night at a comfortable scenic guesthouse or hotel; step out at night to stroll, listen to nature's wind and insects, and look up at the clear, light-pollution-free starry sky—that is Alishan's truest soul.

Zenium A Century-Old Forest Railway Fully Reopens: History, the Four Great Spiral Works & Ticketing Explained

The Alishan Forest Railway was first built in 1912 (Meiji 45 during the Japanese era), stretching 71.4 km. It is not only Taiwan's sole mountain narrow-gauge railway but also gathers the world's four great railway engineering methods to conquer the harsh alpine terrain:the Independent Mountain Spiral Line(climbing by circling the mountain three times),the switchbackI don't know.the special Shay steam locomotive with vertical cylinders, and a vertical climb in just a few dozen kilometers from tropical longan and bamboo forests all the way up to temperate red-cypress giant-tree forests.

Zenium How Old Are the Trees in This Forest? The Science of Giant-Tree Ages & Alpine Ecology

Past travel books often labeled the sacred trees "two thousand or three thousand years old." In recent years, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency and academic teams have drilled tree cores with professional increment borers and combined DNA testing, confirming that most red-cypress sacred trees are actually "composite giants" formed by the fusion of multiple seedling root systems, and have published rigorous, scientifically accurate ages:

Giant Tree Name / Number Species Scientifically Verified Age Previous Estimated Age Trail Location & Highlights
Giant Tree No. 2 Red Cypress About 1,515 years(the park's oldest) No scientific record First section of the Giant Tree boardwalk; trunk girth reaches 12.3 meters, towering and majestic.
Xianglin Sacred Tree (Guangwu Cypress) Red Cypress About 626 years Previously overestimated at 2,300 years Above Shouzhen Temple, beside Ci'en Temple, formed by the fusion of two red cypresses—the park's second-generation sacred tree.
Shuishan Giant Tree Red Cypress About 1,081 years Previously estimated at 1,200 years Walk 1.6 km along the abandoned Shuishan railway; few visitors, hailed as the most serene sacred tree.
Thousand-Year Cypress Red Cypress About 821 years Previously overestimated at 2,000 years A must-pass on the Giant Tree boardwalk; its forked branches rise like hands lifted to the sky in prayer—strikingly dramatic.

Zenium Complete Sunrise-Chasing Guide: Xiaoliyuan 360-Degree Panorama vs. Zhushan Viewing Platform

Zhushan Viewing Platform (Classic Front-of-Station)

• Walking time: 1 minute on foot from Zhushan Railway Station.
• Advantages: exit quickly, with on-site restrooms and hot-drink tea-egg vendors—ideal for elders or young children.
• Disadvantages: extremely dense crowds; photos are easily blocked by front-row crowds and tree canopies, with a dawn view angle of about 180 degrees.

⭐ Xiaoliyuan Viewing Platform (Top Recommendation)

• Walking time: after exiting Zhushan, walk gently uphill along the boardwalk for about 12–15 minutes.
• Advantages: boasts a full, unobstructed 360-degree panorama! Facing Yushan Main Peak, golden light spills over the ridge at dawn; with luck, you may spot the national-treasure Mikado pheasant foraging by the grassy slope.
• Disadvantages: early-morning temperatures are only 6–10°C, and the boardwalk is slightly slippery with dew—bring a windproof warm hat and grippy athletic shoes.
